meta.titre: Market Structures: how the number of sellers shapes price and output
meta.sous_theme: Perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition and monopsony

sections.contenu_markdown: In a busy open-air market, dozens of traders sell almost the same tomatoes, and a buyer simply walks to the next stall if one price is too high. In many towns, by contrast, only one organisation supplies piped water, so households cannot shop around. The number of sellers and buyers, and how alike their products are, change how prices are set and how much power a seller has. The GCE papers regularly ask you to name a market situation from a short description and to compare the main types.

items: A market is any arrangement in which buyers and sellers deal with one another.
A firm is an organisation that produces goods or services to sell.
Revenue from sales equals price multiplied by quantity sold.
A substitute is a good that can be used in place of another.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Comparing the structures

| Structure | Sellers | Product | Entry of new firms | Control over price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perfect competition | Very many | Identical | Free | None: price taker |
| Monopoly | One | No close substitute | Blocked | Large: price maker |
| Oligopoly | A few large ones | Identical or differentiated | Difficult | Some, but rivals react |
| Monopolistic competition | Many | Differentiated | Fairly free | A little |

**Perfect competition** also needs buyers and sellers who know the prices in the market. Each firm sells at the going price and cannot change it alone.

**Product differentiation** means making a product seem different from its rivals through a brand name, packaging, advertising or location, even when the goods are very alike.

**Barriers to entry** keep new firms out: patents and licences, control of raw materials, very large start-up capital, big economies of scale, or the law.

### On the buyers' side

A **monopsony** has only one buyer of a good or of a kind of labour. A **duopoly** has two sellers. Words ending in -opsony refer to buyers; words ending in -opoly refer to sellers.

### Revenue

$$AR = \frac{TR}{Q} = \text{price} \qquad MR = \text{change in } TR \text{ from selling one more unit}$$

A perfectly competitive firm sells every unit at the same price, so $MR = AR = $ price. A monopolist faces a falling demand curve: to sell one more unit it must lower the price, so $MR$ is below the price.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks about a single seller
variantes.contenu_markdown: Monopoly can arise from a patent, a government licence, control of a key raw material or very large size. **Merits**: lower costs through large-scale production, funds for research, and one supplier may suit services such as a water network. **Demerits**: higher price and smaller output than under competition, little choice and weaker pressure to improve. A monopolist that charges different prices for the same product to different buyers practises **price discrimination**.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When firms have rivals but also some power
variantes.contenu_markdown: In **oligopoly** each firm must consider how its few rivals will react, so prices tend to stay fixed and firms rely on advertising and branding; firms may also agree to fix prices, called **collusion**. In **monopolistic competition** many small firms, such as hairdressers or tailors, compete by offering slightly different goods and services.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes a single buyer
variantes.contenu_markdown: A single buyer can pay low prices to suppliers or low wages to workers, because sellers have nowhere else to go. For example, if one factory were the only buyer of a crop in a district, farmers would have to accept its price.

sections.enonce_markdown:
(a) State four features of perfect competition.

(b) Explain two differences between monopoly and perfect competition.

(c) A monopolist faces this demand schedule:

| Quantity | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price (FCFA) | 900 | 800 | 700 | 600 | 500 |

Calculate total revenue and marginal revenue at each quantity.

etapes.justification: "State" needs short points; "explain" needs a reason; "calculate" needs working.
etapes.resultat_markdown: (a) four short points; (b) two differences, each with a reason; (c) a table of TR and MR.

etapes.justification: These are the standard conditions of the model.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Many buyers and sellers; identical products; free entry and exit; buyers and sellers know the prices.

etapes.justification: Each contrast pairs a monopoly fact with a competition fact and gives a consequence.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Number of sellers: one against very many. Price: the monopolist is a price maker because no close rival exists, while the competitive firm is a price taker.

etapes.justification: MR is the change in TR when one more unit is sold.
etapes.resultat_markdown: 900, 700, 500, 300, 100 FCFA. MR is below price after the first unit because the price had to fall on every unit sold.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) Many buyers and sellers; identical products; free entry and exit; good knowledge of prices. (b) A monopoly has one seller and sets the price, while a competitive firm is one of very many and must accept the market price. (c) TR is **900, 1,600, 2,100, 2,400, 2,500 FCFA** and MR is **900, 700, 500, 300, 100 FCFA**.

items.erreur_markdown: "A monopolist can charge any price and still sell as much as it likes."
items.pourquoi_faux: The demand curve slopes downwards: a higher price means fewer sales.
items.correction_markdown: A monopolist can choose the price or the quantity, not both freely.

items.erreur_markdown: "Monopolistic competition is another name for monopoly."
items.pourquoi_faux: It has many sellers with differentiated products and fairly free entry; monopoly has one seller.
items.correction_markdown: Say: many competing firms, each with a slightly different product.

items.pourquoi_faux: With few large sellers, each firm's decision affects the others, which is why they are interdependent.
items.correction_markdown: Oligopolists watch their rivals; they may avoid price cuts or collude.

items.erreur_markdown: "Product differentiation means the products really differ in quality."
items.pourquoi_faux: Differences may be only brand name, packaging or advertising.
items.correction_markdown: Differentiation is making products appear different so that buyers do not see them as perfect substitutes.

items.erreur_markdown: "A monopsony is a market with one seller."
items.correction_markdown: Monopoly has one seller; monopsony has one buyer.

items.enonce_markdown:
Name the market structure described in each case.

(a) A small town has one bakery, and the next one is far away.

(b) Three large firms supply almost all the cement sold in a region.

(c) A single factory is the only buyer of pineapples from growers in a district.

(d) Hundreds of hairdressers, each with a different shop name and style, serve the same city.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Monopoly** (one seller).

(b) **Oligopoly** (few large sellers).

(c) **Monopsony** (one buyer).

(d) **Monopolistic competition** (many sellers with differentiated services).

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) What are barriers to entry? Give two examples.

(b) Explain two ways in which consumers may suffer in a market dominated by one seller.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Barriers to entry are obstacles that stop new firms from joining a market. Examples: **a patent or licence** and **very large start-up capital** (or control of raw materials).

(b) Award marks for two points with reasons: with no rivals the seller can charge a **higher price** and supply less than under competition; consumers have **little choice** and the seller has less pressure to improve quality.

items.enonce_markdown:
A perfectly competitive firm sells at a market price of 400 FCFA per unit. A monopolist faces the demand schedule below.

| Quantity | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price (FCFA) | 600 | 550 | 500 | 450 | 400 |

(a) Calculate total revenue and marginal revenue for the competitive firm for 1 to 5 units.

(b) Calculate total revenue and marginal revenue for the monopolist.

(c) Explain why the monopolist's marginal revenue is below its price while the competitive firm's is not.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $TR = 400, 800, 1200, 1600, 2000$ FCFA; $MR = $ **400 FCFA** for every unit.

(b) $TR = 600, 1100, 1500, 1800, 2000$ FCFA. $MR = $ **600, 500, 400, 300, 200 FCFA**.

(c) The competitive firm can sell more at the same market price, so each extra unit adds exactly the price. The monopolist faces the whole market demand and must lower the price on all units to sell one more, so the extra revenue is the new price minus the revenue lost on earlier units; MR is therefore below price. At 5 units both firms have the same total revenue, 2,000 FCFA, but the monopolist's MR (200) is far below the price (400).

items_markdown: Market structures differ by the number of sellers, the type of product, the ease of entry and the power over price.
Perfect competition: many sellers, identical goods, free entry, price taker. Monopoly: one seller, barriers to entry, price maker.
Oligopoly has a few large interdependent sellers; monopolistic competition has many sellers with differentiated products.
Monopsony means a single buyer; monopoly means a single seller.
Product differentiation uses brands, packaging and advertising; barriers to entry include patents, licences and large capital.
